Trait-gradient analysis

Source: R/trait_gradient.R
trait_gradient.Rd

Splits the trait value of each species into a position along the gradient of community trait means (\(\beta\)) and a difference from the species it co-occurs with (\(\alpha\)), as in the trait-gradient analysis of Ackerly & Cornwell (2007), with three changes: the mean of each site leaves out the focal species, the weights of the site means and of the species means are chosen separately, and trait_gradient_test() and trait_gradient_phylo() give a null model that keeps the richness of sites and the frequency of species and a phylogenetic model that carries the error of \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\).

Usage

trait_gradient(
  data,
  trait = "trait",
  site = "site",
  species = "species",
  abundance = NULL,
  site_weights = if (is.null(abundance)) "occurrence" else "abundance",
  species_weights = site_weights,
  leave_one_out = TRUE,
  min_slope = 3
)

Arguments

data

Data frame with one row per individual or per population (species in a site), such as from sample_individuals(). Rows of one population are averaged.

trait

Name of the column with trait values.

site, species

Names of the columns with the site and the species.

abundance

Name of the column with the abundance of the species in the site (one value per population), or NULL to weight each occurrence equally.

site_weights, species_weights

"abundance" or "occurrence": weights of the site means and of the species means and \(\beta\). Both default to "abundance" when abundance is given.

leave_one_out

Leave the focal species out of the site means (the default).

min_slope

Smallest number of sites with measured values to fit the slope \(b_i\).

Value

An object of class mc_trait_gradient, a list with

species

one row per species: species, n_sites, n_alone (sites where the species is the only species; left out of its values when leave_one_out = TRUE), mean (\(\bar t_i\)), beta, alpha, breadth (\(R_i\)), slope (\(b_i\)), slope_se, intercept and min_site, max_site (range of the site means of its sites).

sites

one row per site: site, n_species and mean (\(p_j\), with all species).

populations

one row per population: site, species, abundance (1 without abundance), weight (the weight of the population in the species means), trait (with species means filled in), measured and site_mean (\(p_j\), or \(p_j^{(-i)}\)).

settings

the arguments.

Details

With \(t_{ij}\) the trait value of species \(i\) in site \(j\) and \(a_{ij}\) its weight, the mean of site \(j\) is $$p_j = \frac{\sum_i a_{ij} t_{ij}}{\sum_i a_{ij}},$$ the mean of species \(i\) is \(\bar t_i = \sum_j a_{ij} t_{ij} / \sum_j a_{ij}\), its position along the gradient is $$\beta_i = \frac{\sum_j a_{ij} p_j}{\sum_j a_{ij}}$$ and its difference from the co-occurring species is \(\alpha_i = \bar t_i - \beta_i\). The niche breadth \(R_i\) is the range of \(p_j\) over the sites of the species and the slope \(b_i\) is the weighted regression of \(t_{ij}\) on \(p_j\), the response of the species to the gradient within its range.

The three changes

Leave-one-out site means. In the original analysis \(p_j\) includes the focal species, so \(\beta_i\) contains \(\bar t_i\): in sites with few species, \(\beta\) follows the trait of the species itself, and \(\beta\) is correlated with \(\bar t\) and with \(\alpha\) even when traits are unrelated to where species live. With leave_one_out = TRUE (the default) \(\beta_i\), \(R_i\) and \(b_i\) use \(p_j^{(-i)} = (\sum_{k \ne i} a_{kj} t_{kj}) / \sum_{k \ne i} a_{kj}\), and sites where species \(i\) is the only species are left out of its values (counted in n_alone). The jackknife of the original script does the same, as an option; leave_one_out = FALSE gives the original values.

Leaving the species out does not make the raw correlation of \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) readable on its own. Because \(\alpha = \bar t - \beta\), without any assembly the correlation is negative, near \(-sd(\beta) / sd(\alpha)\), whereas with the focal species in the site means it is positive. Read it against a null model, as its standardised effect size in trait_gradient_test().

Weights. The weights of the site means (site_weights) and of the species means and \(\beta\) (species_weights) are chosen apart, as abundance or occurrence; the original uses one choice for both. Compare the two with trait_gradient_weights().

Null model and error. See trait_gradient_test() and trait_gradient_phylo().

Trait values missing in a site where the species occurs (NA in trait, with the row kept) are replaced by the mean of the species, as in the original; the slope \(b_i\) uses only measured values.

References

Ackerly, D. D., & Cornwell, W. K. (2007). A trait-based approach to community assembly: partitioning of species trait values into within- and among-community components. Ecology Letters, 10, 135–145. doi:10.1111/j.1461-0248.2006.01006.x

Examples

set.seed(1)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(20)
sim <- simulate_metacommunity(landscape_implicit(15), species_traits(tree),
                              competition_matrix(tree, "none"), n_steps = 100,
                              seed_steps = 1:5)
ind <- sample_individuals(sim, n = 5, local_adaptation = 0.5, intraspecific_sd = 1)
tg <- trait_gradient(ind, abundance = "abundance")
head(tg$species)
#>   species n_sites n_alone      mean     beta       alpha  breadth     slope
#> 1      t1       3       0 67.956541 67.41152   0.5450167 28.45005 0.6848220
#> 2     t10      15       0 51.064276 52.59265  -1.5283787 70.25170 0.6234984
#> 3     t11       4       0 60.927325 61.58517  -0.6578440 21.75283 0.6590566
#> 4     t12       2       0 64.591689 65.46605  -0.8743607 14.06901        NA
#> 5     t13      12       0 29.407255 45.42789 -16.0206324 70.45406 0.3865279
#> 6     t15       1       0  4.898275 22.26285 -17.3645737  0.00000        NA
#>      slope_se intercept min_site max_site
#> 1 0.003962136  21.79165 44.54802 72.99807
#> 2 0.020972694  18.27284 12.66171 82.91341
#> 3 0.050671341  20.33921 51.35616 73.10899
#> 4          NA        NA 51.61021 65.67922
#> 5 0.053463943  11.84811 10.26715 80.72121
#> 6          NA        NA 22.26285 22.26285
# the original, with the focal species in the site means
original <- trait_gradient(ind, abundance = "abundance", leave_one_out = FALSE)
head(cbind(leave_one_out = tg$species$beta, original = original$species$beta))
#>      leave_one_out original
#> [1,]      67.41152 67.45006
#> [2,]      52.59265 52.65582
#> [3,]      61.58517 61.55826
#> [4,]      65.46605 65.38875
#> [5,]      45.42789 37.71938
#> [6,]      22.26285 12.75160
